intro: At Madrid’s Museum of Romanticism, with no audience in the room, Patrizia Prati plays Chopin’s E♭-major Nocturne in November 2015. The left hand keeps its easy tread while the tune gathers ornaments and finally takes off on its own.

sections.label: A · Song above bass and chords
sections.mNote: Four slow beats to a bar, each divided into three

sections.label: B · Repeated E♭s, then a rising tune
sections.mNote: The bass descends through B♭, A♮ and A♭

sections.label: C · Minor chords and climbing octaves
sections.mNote: A♭-minor harmony prepares the final ascent and cadenza

sections.label: Coda · Soft chords in E♭
sections.mNote: The first tempo returns after the free cadenza

cues.title: Three steps beneath each beat
cues.text: The left hand places a low note, then two chords: three steps beneath each slow beat. Above it the melody rises from B♭ to G. Chopin asks for espressivo dolce, expressive and sweet.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), upbeat and opening bar, 12/8 and espressivo dolce. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A pianist between languages
cues.text: Prati studies piano with Giancarlo Cardini, Aldo Ciccolini and András Schiff, and harpsichord with Anna Maria Pernafelli. Her work also takes her to the writing desk: she publishes on music, literature and literary translation.
cues.evidence: Patrizia Prati’s curriculum vitae, pp. 1–2, lists these teachers and her writing on literary translation: https://patriziaprati.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Patrizia-Prati-CV-IT.pdf

cues.title: The bass walks down
cues.text: A new phrase starts on F, rises to G and sinks back. Underneath, the bass steps down from B♭ to A♮, then A♭. The right hand repeats E♭ softly, taking its time over the descent.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 9–10: F–G–F melody, descending B♭–A♮–A♭ bass and repeated E♭s. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The song comes back embroidered
cues.text: A quick sweep through G, B♭ and E♭ brings the melody back to its high G. This version has more twists, trills and accented little notes. The left hand resumes the familiar pattern under the returning tune.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 21–24, the last varied statement of the opening theme. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The coda keeps E♭
cues.text: The tune pares itself down to E♭, F and G. An A♭-minor chord gives its opening a sudden shadow; the bass keeps E♭ underneath. Soon the melody climbs again, marked ever more softly.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 25–28: Coda, tonic bass, minor-subdominant harmony, pp and sempre pp. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The accompaniment stops walking
cues.text: The bass climbs through a B♭-dominant chord and holds it. Above, the high octaves pause, then the right hand spins a four-note figure. Senza tempo leaves this little cadenza free of the old tread.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bar 32: dominant arpeggio, fermata and senza tempo cadenza. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The final rocking chords
cues.text: E♭ returns in the bass beneath gently rocking chords. The piano is marked pp, then ppp. After all the right hand’s flights, the nocturne ends with three plain chords, the last held beneath a fermata.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 33–34: Tempo I, pp, ppp and final fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The bass descends beneath repeated E♭s
transitions.from: A · Song above bass and chords
transitions.to: B · Repeated E♭s, then a rising tune
transitions.how: The bass steps down through B♭, A♮ and A♭ while the right hand repeats E♭. Over A♭, a major chord turns minor when C falls to C♭. The bass then reaches E♭; the melody falls to B♭ before leaping up an octave into the next phrase.

transitions.title: A♭ minor beneath the last ascent
transitions.from: B · Repeated E♭s, then a rising tune
transitions.to: C · Minor chords and climbing octaves
transitions.how: A♭-minor chords return, now with A♭ itself deep in the bass. The right hand turns around E♭ and F before climbing under the marking con forza. High octaves take over the melody, pressing towards the B♭ dominant chord on which the cadenza will hang.

transitions.title: A free run reaches E♭
transitions.from: C · Minor chords and climbing octaves
transitions.how: The final run descends over the held B♭ dominant seventh, ending with C and D. E♭ follows in both hands, resolving the chord. Tempo I restores the first pace, and the piano rolls through E♭ major, softly, before the last three chords.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
